title: Pre-stage Windows devices for Autopilot: hardware hash import vs corporate identifiers, by CSV or Graph
problem: Classic Autopilot needs a registered hardware hash; device preparation with personal enrollment blocked needs a corporate identifier instead. Mixing them up is the most common reason a new device enrolls as personal, gets blocked, or runs the wrong flow.
steps: Decide per fleet: classic Autopilot profile = register the hardware hash (ideally by OEM/reseller, own upload mainly for test and limited cases). Device preparation = no registration; upload a Windows corporate identifier (manufacturer, model, serial) only if an enrollment restriction blocks personal Windows devices, or use device association.

Collect a hash on a running device (elevated): `Install-Script -Name Get-WindowsAutopilotInfo` then `Get-WindowsAutopilotInfo -OutputFile AutopilotHWID.csv`. In OOBE: Shift+F10, `powershell.exe`, then `Get-WindowsAutopilotInfo -Online` with an Intune Administrator (first run asks for Graph consent). Windows 11 OOBE can also export it from the diagnostics page (Ctrl+Shift+D).

Merge into one CSV, max 500 rows per batch, header exactly `Device Serial Number,Windows Product ID,Hardware Hash,Group Tag,Assigned User`: no extra columns, no quotes, ANSI encoding, edited in a plain-text editor, never saved from Excel.
Import: Intune admin center > Devices > Windows > Enrollment > Windows Autopilot > Devices > Import, then Sync and Refresh until the rows appear. Wait for each batch to finish before the next.

Scripted import: `POST https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/deviceManagement/importedWindowsAutopilotDeviceIdentities/import` with `importedWindowsAutopilotDeviceIdentities[]` carrying `serialNumber`, `hardwareIdentifier` (Base64 hash), optional `groupTag` and `assignedUserPrincipalName`. Permission: `DeviceManagementServiceConfig.ReadWrite.All`. Poll `state.deviceImportStatus` and `deviceErrorName`.

Verify registrations: `GET https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/deviceManagement/windowsAutopilotDeviceIdentities` (filter on serial) and confirm each device has the intended group tag and an assigned profile.

Corporate identifiers for Windows: build a CSV without header, one `Manufacturer,Model,Serial` line per device (periods removed from the serial, max 5,000 rows / 5 MB, one identifier type per file). Read the values with `Get-CimInstance Win32_ComputerSystem | ForEach-Object { $_.Manufacturer, $_.Model, (Get-CimInstance Win32_BIOS).SerialNumber -join ',' }`.

Upload: Devices > Enrollment > Corporate device identifiers > Add > Upload CSV file > Manufacturer, model, and serial number (Windows only). Manual entry isn't available for Windows. Above 10 CSV uploads, use Graph: `POST https://graph.microsoft.com/beta/deviceManagement/importedDeviceIdentities/importDeviceIdentityList` (beta) with `DeviceManagementServiceConfig.ReadWrite.All`.
Only now enable or confirm the device platform restriction that blocks personally owned Windows devices, and track identifier status (Enrolled, Not contacted, Failed).
pitfalls: Windows corporate identifiers only matter at enrollment time. Afterwards Intune shows ownership from normal Windows logic, so a device can enroll as corporate and later read Personal; fix it in device Properties if you need to.
Once any Windows corporate identifier exists, every other Entra join during setup is marked personal. Uploading a partial list and then blocking personal devices locks out the rest of the fleet.
Corporate identifiers need Windows 11 22H2/23H2 builds 22621.3374/22631.3374 or later (Windows 10 22H2 19045.4598). Older builds report model and manufacturer as Unknown and never match.

Microsoft recommends uploading 4K hashes yourself only for testing or limited cases: the hash carries sensitive hardware data and loosely vetted Intune accounts exist. Prefer OEM/partner registration, and treat exported CSVs as secrets that you delete after import.
Don't register Entra registered (workplace joined) or MDM-only devices as Autopilot devices; remove them from Intune and Entra first or the join type sticks as registered.
An invalid UPN in Assigned User isn't validated beyond the domain and can make the device unusable until the assignment is removed.
done_when: Every classic-Autopilot device appears under Windows Autopilot devices with the right group tag and an assigned profile.
Every device-preparation device that needs it is listed under Corporate device identifiers before first boot.
A test device enrolls as Corporate and is not stopped by the personal-device restriction.

troubleshooting.symptom: Import does nothing, network trace shows HTTP 400 'Cannot convert the literal ... to Edm.Binary'.
troubleshooting.fix: Test with `[Convert]::FromBase64String("<hash>")` and adjust trailing `=`/`A` padding until it decodes, then re-import.
The hash is registered in another tenant; the other tenant (or the reseller) must deregister it first.
Search the serial under Windows Autopilot devices; drop duplicate rows instead of importing again.
Manufacturer or serial is empty in the hash. Check `Get-CimInstance Win32_BaseBoard | Select-Object Manufacturer, SerialNumber`.

troubleshooting.symptom: Enrollment fails with Enrollment restriction not met.
troubleshooting.fix: Check Devices > Enrollment failures, then confirm the identifier triple matches what the device reports (exact model string, serial without periods).

rollback: If devices are blocked after enabling the personal-device restriction, set Windows (MDM) personally owned back to Allow in that restriction first; that is the fastest reversible state.
Delete wrong corporate identifiers under Corporate device identifiers. Deleting doesn't change ownership of already enrolled devices.

To undo a hash registration: delete the device from Intune first, unassign the user, then delete it under Windows Autopilot devices and Sync. For Entra joined devices, don't delete the Entra object by hand.
Confirm the undo: the serial no longer appears in `windowsAutopilotDeviceIdentities`, and a test device enrolls or runs the intended flow.
